reference_items.subject: Mathematics
reference_items.stem:
Sam said that 1/3 of a pie is less than 1/4 of the same pie.

Is Sam correct? ____

Use the circles below to show why this is so.

[Image: Two circles]

Shade in 1/3 of this circle

Shade in 1/4 of this circle

descriptors: NO. Both circles are correctly partitioned.
NO. No partitioning is shown.
NO. Only one of the circles correctly partitioned.
NO. Other incorrect ways of partitioning.
YES, or there is no conclusion stated. Both circles are correctly partitioned.
Other partial.
YES. No partitioning is shown.
YES. The part representing 1/3 is made consistently smaller than the part representing 1/4.
YES. Other responses where one or both of the circles partitioned into 3 and/or 4 parts.
Other incorrect.

reference_items.scoring_notes: Note: The partition of circles has priority over shading. This is reflected in the scoring guide below.

reference_items.subject: Mathematics
reference_items.stem:
This chart shows the types of cookies sold by the local bakery.

[Image: Pie chart titled Cookies Sold, shaded and divided into various sizes; sugar about one-fourth, chocolate chip more than one-fourth, oatmeal more than one-half, and vanilla about one-eighth.]

Which type of cookie did the bakery sell the most of?
reference_items.figure_description:
A pie chart titled "Cookies Sold" is divided into four unequal sectors:
- "sugar": light-gray shading, occupying the top-right quadrant from the 12 o'clock position to the 3 o'clock position (a right angle, exactly one-quarter of the circle).
- "chocolate chip": medium-gray shading, occupying the sector from the 3 o'clock position to approximately the 5 o'clock position.
- "oatmeal": white (unshaded), occupying the largest sector from approximately the 5 o'clock position counter-clockwise around the bottom and left to approximately the 10:30 position.
- "vanilla": white (unshaded), occupying the sector from approximately the 10:30 position to the 12 o'clock position.
Visually, oatmeal is the largest sector, sugar is the second largest, chocolate chip is third, and vanilla is the smallest.

slope.instructions: TIMSS scaled this 1-point item with the two-parameter logistic (2PL) model, which TIMSS uses for constructed-response items worth 1 point, in the calibration "Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2003 data, 2007 bridging data, and 2007 data (fourth-grade mathematics)". What is the item's slope (discrimination) parameter a? A higher a means that the item separates students of lower and higher mathematics ability more sharply. Choose the value closest to it. The state also lists reference items: the calibrated TIMSS items of the same grade most similar to this one (never the item itself or its other parts), most similar first, with their percent correct and their calibrated parameters, each on the scale of its own calibration. Use them to place this item.
